utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody in the court. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution, assisted by Alma Imamovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP, everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic, Nicholas Robson, on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Lejla Gluhic is our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Trivicevic, yesterday you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I just want to warn you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson, if I'm not mistaken, you had finished your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to a question that I asked you at page 23 and 24, you told us about the one time you were interrogated at Livade, and in response to a question from my colleague Mr. Robson for the Defence, at pages 90 and 91 you told us about being interrogated at KP Dom Zenica. Other than these two instances, on how many occasions, if any, were you interrogated during the time period that you were detained from 21 July 1995 until 7 January 1996?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another round of interrogation, and that's when we were being held by the Mujahedin. If I remember correctly, that was on the 4th of August, 1995, when they took us out one by one and took us up to the first floor, blindfolded. We were interrogated blindfolded, therefore. They beat us with plastic pipes, the sort of pipe used for water pipes. That was the last thing I wanted to say. And if I may just say something about the interrogation in Zenica. We started speaking about that towards the end of yesterday's session. That interrogation was conducted under threat and duress. When I came there to provide my statement, the investigator Edo Sabic or whatever his name was told me to watch my words. Should he not be satisfied with my statement, he said he could easily arrange for me to be sent right back where I'd come from. Likewise, when the Red Cross listed us, which was on the 31st of December, a guard walked into the room and said that the Red Cross officials would be on their way to take our names down, but under no conditions should we ever mention anything about the existence of the El Mujahedin Detachment; one thing we ought to know is that it was by no means self-implicit that everyone would be released from captivity. He said should anyone asked who we had been captured by, we should say that it was some sort of an assault group from the BH Army, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivicevic. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The numbers of the Mujahedin Detachment, in the first place where you were detained, in the camp that you described to us, I'd like to know whether those members were all foreigners or whether also local members of the Mujahedin, local Muslims who spoke your language.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The El Mujahedin unit also comprised local Muslims, people who spoke our language and were members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Habib, who showed a degree of humanity towards you, was he a foreign Mujahedin member who didn't speak your language?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke our language very poorly, but we were able to establish some sort of communication. He told us he was 17 and that he came from South Yemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then there's another thing as well. You said that there were people who came to transfer you. I understood, and actually I'd like your confirmation that I understood correctly, that these were Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were Bosnians. They had come twice before already. The third time they came, it was because of the Mujahedin, that they transferred us to the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they managed to get into the camp without any difficulty. What were their relations with the foreign Mujahedin? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how they got into the camp. I was locked up in a room that had all the windows boarded up. The relations with the Mujahedin were at a very high level, were very good. They had asked to go in and look at the Chetnik prisoners, and the Mujahedin would simply let them in, allow them to access the room. Having received approval from the Mujahedin, they got some spades. They would remove the last part of the spade and keep the stick, which they would use to hit us. They would tread on us with their boots and lash out at us in all sorts of ways. However, whenever the Mujahedin guard mentioned the word "emr," which we didn't know, I thought it was some sort of order or something like that, but as soon as he uttered this word, they would automatically stop beating us and leave the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trivicevic, I wanted to explore the registration a bit with you. You said you were registered finally on 31st December by the ICRC in Zenica, I suppose. Is that correct? Were you ever registered before that time? What I wish to know is whether at any point you were asked to give your name and your rank to anyone after your imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened every time we were interrogated. Our names were taken down, our statements likewise, all our personal details, the details of our units and so on and so forth, the first time at Livade and the second time when we were taken up to that first floor in that house in which we were being held, and the third time a list was drawn up two or three days after our arrival at the KP Dom in Zenica. The fourth time around, International Red Cross people came and they took our names down. That's as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the statements you gave during the interrogations were recorded, or written down, or noted somehow?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement at Livade was written down. I did actually see people take it down, take down what we were saying. As for the one taken at the camp, on the upper floor of that house in which we were being held, I don't know. I had a blindfold on, I couldn't see anything. As for the statement at the KP Dom in Zenica, there's a statement that I wrote in my own hand. I told you about the circumstances under which this happened. Every time I wrote down a sentence, I had to share this sentence with the investigator first. If he didn't like it, he would say, "No, don't write that, you can't write that. Write this or write that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if your statements taken in Livade was ever passed on to the ABiH? Or in other words, sir, do you know what happened to your statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no idea what became of any of the statements that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question relating to your transfer from Kamenica to Zenica, and I'm curious to know if you know how this was arranged. What sort of cooperation would there have been between the El Mujahid Detachment and the ABiH authorities in Zenica to allow for this transfer? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I know is about the circumstances, how we were taken away, how we were transported to Zenica, and how we eventually got there. I have no idea what happened at the higher levels of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the level of cooperation and coordination between the leadership in Kamenica, the Mujahid leadership, and the military authorities in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really know nothing about the level of their cooperation. I did see people from the army several times at the Mujahedin camp and at Livade. I don't know what prompted their visits and what sort of cooperation this was exactly. I wasn't able to learn at the time, nor did I ever get any opportunity to learn about this later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Trivicevic, you mentioned yesterday that somebody, and I think it was a young man, who cut your ears. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he cut them off or did he only scar them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite obvious that both my ears are still where they're supposed to be, but he made half circles on my ears with a small jackknife, a pocket knife. He sliced up both my ears, but not cut them off entirely, as is obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you mind removing the headphones for a moment?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I might, but it's very difficult to actually spot this the scars from this sort of distance. Those were small cuts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then that's fine. Okay, thank you very much. Can we have Exhibit 552 on the screen, please. Mr. Trivicevic, I just want you to have a good look at this document on the screen. I think I heard you yesterday say that you wrote it yourself. I just want you to double-check and confirm that, indeed, you did. And the reason I do so is because it is dated the 26th of August, 1995, but then it says "Official Note," and I don't know whether you would be giving an official note or it will be an official who would give the official note. And then it says: "Made on the 25th ..." This seems to be a record of something that was done the previous day. Do you confirm that this is your own document?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know about this document is the general things that are stated in it. I know about the circumstances. I had a pen and paper in front of me. I wrote down the statement myself. I don't know whether it was copied later on or what it was used for. I really don't know how the statement was used at any of the later stages of its life. I was inside a cell. I really didn't know what was going on at the command post or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you sign the statement that you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed the statement that I wrote down myself alone. I don't remember about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the statement that you signed, was it typed or was it written by pen?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hand-wrote the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you ever shown the statement after it had been typed, or do you -- well, we see this one is typed. Were you ever shown a typed statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that statement again, nor did I ever go to the Zenica KP Dom Command building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just have a look at the end of the statement, particularly the B/C/S, and see whether it's signed. I see a signature there. Is that yours?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR TRIVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you. Thank you so much, sir. Any questions arising, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings us to the end of your testimony, sir. Thank you so much for taking time off to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And may I add, sir -- excuse me. May I add our sympathy and compassion for the pain and hardship that you went through and your courage to come here and tell about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank everyone who has had the goodwill to listen to my statement, to hear out what I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. You may stand down, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, Mr. Mundis, that brings us to the end of the day for the business for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It does indeed, Your Honours, and I will indicate for the record that the schedule, as previously circulated, remains unchanged for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, we adjourn to Monday, the 8th of October, at 9.00, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.25 a.m.,
